---
title: "The reader experience"
---

A qmd-fast page is not just rendered HTML, it is a reading surface. Every built
page carries a suite of reader tools behind a single **Aa** control in the
bottom-right corner. They need no author configuration: they appear on every
article automatically (slide decks have their own chrome, so they are skipped).

Two principles hold for everything on this page:

- **Reader-side and read-only.** Each tool stores its state in the *reader's own*
  browser `localStorage`, keyed by the page path. Nothing is written back to your
  `.qmd` source, and nothing leaves the browser. This is the single-editing-surface
  rule applied to the output: the reader owns a reading of the document, the
  document stays authoritative.
- **Exact and durable.** Because every block carries a content-hash
  `data-block-id`, highlights, bookmarks, and reading position anchor to block
  identity, not to fragile scroll offsets or fuzzy text. They survive a re-render
  and a change of window size.

## The reader menu

The **Aa** button opens a light-dismiss popover (not a modal: it never covers or
inerts the page). It hosts every reader tool as a labelled section: Display,
Reading, Highlights, Bookmarks, and Listen. Close it with Esc, a click outside, or
by activating a jump button inside.

## Display preferences

The **Display** section is a comfort suite. Each control is a segmented row, and
every choice persists and is applied *before the page paints*, so a returning
reader never sees a flash of the default:

- **Theme**: Light, Dark, or Sepia.
- **Text size**: small, normal, large, or x-large.
- **Width**: Narrow, Normal, or Wide reading measure.
- **Line spacing**: Tight, Normal, or Relaxed.
- **Letter spacing** and **Word spacing**: Normal, Wide, or Wider. The Wider steps
  meet the WCAG 1.4.12 text-spacing minimums (0.12em letter, 0.16em word), and use
  `em` units so they scale with the chosen text size.

A **Reset to defaults** button clears all six preferences at once.

## Reading progress and resume

For long reads, the **Reading** section answers "how much is left?" and "where was
I?":

- A thin **progress bar** at the top of the page fills as you scroll.
- A **minutes-left readout** estimates the remaining time from the prose word
  count below the cursor (code and equations are excluded), shown as
  `~N min left, X% read`.
- A **Resume reading** pill appears when you reopen a page you left partway
  through. It scrolls you back to the exact block you stopped at, anchored to that
  block's content hash. It dismisses itself after a few seconds or on your next
  scroll.
- On pages with a table of contents, sections you have scrolled through gain a
  **read checkmark** in the TOC, so a long reference page shows your trail at a
  glance.

## Highlights, notes, and bookmarks

Select any prose and a small toolbar appears. Click **Highlight** to mark the
passage; click a mark again to remove it. Highlights are anchored to the block id
plus character offsets in the prose (code and math are skipped), so they persist
across reloads and survive edits to *other* blocks.

When a page has highlights, a **My highlights** entry collects them with jump and
remove buttons, and an **Export as Markdown** action that produces a clean list of
quotes (with the page title and a link) to paste into your notes.

Hovering a heading reveals a **star** in the margin; click it to bookmark the
section. The menu's **Bookmarks** section lists every bookmarked heading for
one-click jumps. Highlights are single-block prose only; bookmarks attach to
headings.

## The selection toolbar

The same selection toolbar carries clipboard actions, all local (no server):

- **Copy**: the plain selected text.
- **Quote**: a Markdown blockquote with the document title and a link.
- **Share link**: a W3C text-fragment URL (`#:~:text=`) that scrolls a reader
  straight to the exact passage and highlights it. (Text fragments do not work over
  `file://`, so the action says so there.)
- **Cite**: a ready-to-paste BibTeX `@misc` entry with the title, a deep link, and
  the access date.

## Hover cross-reference cards

Hovering an internal reference, a `@fig-`/`@sec-`/`@eq-` cross-reference, a `[@cite]`
citation, or a footnote, pops a card showing the *target block itself* (the figure,
the equation, the bibliography entry, or a heading with its first lines). You read
the target without losing your place. The cards render the already-rendered content,
so there is no re-execution, and table-of-contents links are excluded.

## Anchor copy-links

Hovering a heading or a numbered float (figure, table, listing) reveals a small
`#`. Click it to copy the canonical deep link to that anchor. The `#` flashes to a
check on success and announces "Link copied" for screen readers. It works in
insecure contexts (a `--host` LAN preview, `file://`) through a clipboard fallback.

## Focus mode

Press **f** (or use the menu toggle) to enter focus mode: the navbar, footer, TOC,
and sidebar disappear, and the prose centres into one calm column. The progress bar
and the Aa button stay, so you keep your exit paths and your size and theme
controls. Press **f** again or **Esc** to leave. Focus mode is momentary: it is not
remembered across reloads, and the `f` key is ignored while you are typing in a
field or a dialog is open.

## Listen (read-aloud)

The **Listen** control reads the page aloud with the browser's built-in speech, so
it works offline with your operating system's voices. It starts from the block in
view, so press Listen wherever you are.

- **Prose** is read one sentence at a time, with the current sentence highlighted
  and scrolled to the centre.
- **Code** is announced ("Code block, 12 lines, Python") and then its lines light
  up one by one, without reading the code aloud.
- **Figures, equations, and tables** are announced by their caption or number.

A floating mini-player (play/pause, previous/next block, speed, stop) controls
playback without reopening the menu. Your **speed** (0.8x to 2x) and **voice** are
remembered across pages; the playback position itself is momentary. Read-aloud
respects `prefers-reduced-motion` (no smooth scroll when reduced motion is set).

## Keyboard and accessibility

Tab from the top of any page reveals a **Skip to content** link that jumps focus past
the chrome straight to the prose. The link and its focusable `<main>` target are
emitted server-side, so they work even with JavaScript disabled. A handful of keyboard
shortcuts speed up reading (each is ignored while you are typing in a field or a dialog
is open):

- `?` opens (and closes) a shortcuts cheatsheet.
- `/` opens the search palette.
- `f` toggles focus mode.
- `←` / `→` move to the previous / next chapter (in a book).
- `Esc` closes the open menu, dialog, or palette.

Keyboard focus is always visible: every interactive control (links, buttons, tabs,
the reader-menu controls, and the deck controls) shares one consistent focus ring,
shown only for keyboard or assistive-technology focus and never on a mouse click. The
ring is a single theme token, so it follows the active theme (including Sepia and the
high-contrast modes below).

**Landmarks and dialogs.** Each `<nav>` on a page carries a distinguishing accessible
name (the table of contents announces as "Table of contents", separate from the
navbar and the prev/next pager), so a screen reader's landmark list is navigable.
Modal overlays (the search palette, the image viewer, the keyboard cheatsheet) move
focus into themselves on open, trap Tab while open, and restore focus to whatever
opened them on close; the **Aa** reader menu is a light-dismiss popover, so it does
not trap focus but returns it to the **Aa** button when you press Esc.

**Slide decks** announce as you navigate. Each slide is a labelled group ("Slide 3 of
12"), and a polite live region speaks the new position (and its title) on every move,
so a deck is navigable and announceable with a screen reader.

**High contrast.** In Windows High Contrast / `forced-colors` mode, and under
`prefers-contrast: more`, borders, focus rings, separators, and the active-item
markers are re-asserted with system colors so the chrome stays legible when the
palette is forced.

Prose also gets quiet typographic polish that needs no configuration: balanced
headings and captions, pretty last-line wrapping, and figures that keep their caption
attached.
